extracted.intended_audience: regulatory scholars, policymakers, agency officials, law students, and informed public interested in U.S. federal rulemaking and OIRA
extracted.subtask_description: A concise overview of what the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) actually does in reviewing agency rules — its role in inter-agency coordination, causes of delay, the place of cost–benefit analysis, and how it handles public comments and legal issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-agency review and use of agency specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA helps to oversee a genuinely inter-agency process involving lots of specialists throughout the federal government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The people who are reviewing rules are predominantly outside of OIRA; e.g., EPA will scrutinize transportation rules for environmental impacts, USDA will analyze agricultural impacts of EPA rules, OSTP will contribute scientific expertise for Interior rules. OIRA's goal is often to identify and convey inter-agency reviews to seek a reasonable consensus; it operates as a conveyor and a convener.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delays usually reflect unresolved inter-agency concerns needing consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proposed or final rule is delayed and the OIRA process is time consuming, it is often because a significant inter-agency concern hasn’t been addressed and there is not yet consensus within the administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delays commonly arise from substantive objections (legal or policy) from other parts of the Executive Branch that must be worked through rather than from slipshod or purely political review. Examples include legal objections from DOJ or technical policy problems such as inadequate assessment of effects on small businesses. Such delay is presented as a time-consuming but constructive effort to tap expertise and resolve objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs and benefits matter but are not usually the dominant issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost–benefit analysis is important and emphasized by administrations, but it is not the daily, dominant aspect of OIRA's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although outside observers often view OIRA as the home of cost–benefit analysis, in practice CBA is occasional. The office spends more time on other tasks (notably assessing public comments and resolving legal questions). The Council of Economic Advisors and others also focus on costs and benefits, but CBA is one component among several in OIRA's review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful assessment of public comments and ensuring presentation of alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: A central part of OIRA's work is carefully assessing public comments and ensuring that alternatives are raised and discussed so the public can respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'Hayekian' function means OIRA works to make sure, for a proposed rule, that the public is presented with a range of options and can anticipate and correct possible mistakes through the comment process. The emphasis is on surfacing alternatives and enabling meaningful public participation rather than solely focusing on numeric cost–benefit calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement with Executive Branch lawyers to resolve legal questions
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA spends substantial time engaging lawyers throughout the Executive Branch to resolve questions of law; legal compliance is a central, daily concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal objections (for example, DOJ finding a proposed rule unlawful) are a serious impediment to moving forward; addressing legal issues can be a primary reason for extended review. These engagements are distinct from cost–benefit work and often take up more of OIRA's day-to-day attention.
